Name: Adam
Transcript: Thanks for doing this. There are no right answers, it's your experience I'm after, and we can stop at any point. You mentioned when we spoke that she isn't with you now. Can you tell me what it was like, sharing your home with her?

Name: Rowan
Transcript: Yeah. Erm. Where to start. She went in the summer, so I keep starting to say it is and then it's was. Skye. Collie cross, from the rescue, she was about two when I got her. And what it was like. It was everything, really, for about eighteen months. I mean that both ways. She was the first thing I thought about when I woke up and the last thing at night, and most of the bits in between. The flat was her flat. I just lived in it.

Name: Adam
Transcript: You said you mean that both ways.

Name: Rowan
Transcript: Yeah. The good way first. She was the best company I've ever had, honestly, and she came at a point where I didn't have much company. I'd not long split up with someone, I'd moved here, I was working from home, so whole days could go by and I wouldn't speak to anyone. And then there's this dog leaning on my knee under the desk. But the other way is that she took over. Everything had to be arranged round her. Every single thing. And I didn't see it happening until it had already happened.

Name: Adam
Transcript: Can you take me through a day, back when she was with you?

Name: Rowan
Transcript: So I'd be up at quarter past five. Not because she woke me, she'd have slept till nine given the chance, but because the park's empty at half five. That was the whole point. She couldn't cope with other dogs. If she saw one, even right across the park, she'd go up on her back legs and scream at it. Not bark. Scream. And I'd be hanging on to the lead with both hands. So we went when nobody else did. Half five in the morning and then again at eleven at night. Dark at both ends. I used to joke I'd gone nocturnal. I wasn't really joking.

Name: Adam
Transcript: What were those walks in the dark like?

Name: Rowan
Transcript: Some of them were lovely, actually. I don't want to make out it was all, you know. In the winter there'd be frost on the field and nobody about, just us, and she'd be off the lead in the tennis courts, the fenced bit, doing these big loops with her ears inside out. And I'd stand in the middle with my coffee and think, this is all right, this is ours. But I was always listening. Even when she was happy I was listening for a car door, or a jingle, someone else's dog. I never stopped listening, the whole time I had her.

Name: Adam
Transcript: You never stopped listening.

Name: Rowan
Transcript: No. And I didn't notice I was doing it until after. That's the strange bit. A few weeks after she'd gone I was walking to the shop and someone came round the corner with a spaniel and I crossed the road. Just did it. I was halfway across before I thought, what are you doing, you haven't got a dog. My body was still doing it for her.

Name: Adam
Transcript: And in the day, while you were working?

Name: Rowan
Transcript: She'd lie under the desk with her head on my foot. If I moved my foot she'd shuffle round till she found it again. Which is lovely, and it was lovely, but it also meant I couldn't really go anywhere. She couldn't be left. The first time I tried, I went to the supermarket, forty minutes, and the woman downstairs put a note through the door saying she'd howled the whole time. And when I got in she'd had a go at the door frame. Not much, but the paint was off and there were these little teeth marks. So after that I didn't leave her. I mean I didn't leave her at all, for months. I got everything delivered. If I had to go somewhere she came and sat in the car.

Name: Adam
Transcript: How was that for you, not being able to leave her?

Name: Rowan
Transcript: Erm. At the time I'd have said it was fine. I'd have said I'm a homebody anyway. But my sister came up, it must have been nine months in, and she said, you've not been out, have you. Like, out out. And I hadn't. I'd stopped saying yes to things so long ago that people had stopped asking. So it's hard to say what it was like, because I didn't feel it as a loss while it was going on. It was just how things were. I had the dog. The dog was the reason, and it's a good reason, nobody argues with it.

Name: Adam
Transcript: Was there a point where that started to change?

Name: Rowan
Transcript: There was a letter. From the letting agent. One of the other tenants had a little terrier and Skye went for it on the stairs. I had her on the lead, I had her short, but it's narrow and she got past my legs. The terrier was all right, it was a nip on the ear, but there was blood on the carpet and the woman was crying, and then the letter came saying any further incident and they'd have to review the tenancy. And I stood in the hall reading it with Skye leaning on my legs and I thought, I can't keep her safe here. Or I can't keep everyone else safe. One of those.

Name: Adam
Transcript: One of those.

Name: Rowan
Transcript: Yeah. I've gone back and forth on which. At the time I think it was everyone else. Later it was her. That I'd put her in a life she couldn't do. A flat with a shared staircase and a park full of dogs, for a dog who was frightened of all of it. That wasn't her fault. That was mine. I chose the flat and then I chose her, and I never thought about the two together.

Name: Adam
Transcript: What happened next?

Name: Rowan
Transcript: I tried everything first. I want that on the record. There was a behaviourist, she came out three times, she was good, she gave me exercises and I did them every day. Rewarding her for seeing a dog and not going. And it helped a bit. It helped in the park at half five when the other dog was a long way off. It never helped on the stairs. Nothing was going to help on the stairs. And in the end it was the behaviourist who said it, really, very gently. She said some dogs need a different life, not a different owner, and sometimes it's both. And I knew what she meant before she'd finished saying it.

Name: Adam
Transcript: What was it like, hearing that?

Name: Rowan
Transcript: Awful. And a relief. Both at once, and I was ashamed of the relief, I still am a bit. I went quiet for about a week. Didn't do anything about it. I kept taking her out at half five and watching her and thinking, you don't know. You've got no idea I'm thinking this. And she'd be doing her loops round the tennis courts and I felt like I was lying to her. Which is mad, she's a dog. But that's what it felt like.

Name: Adam
Transcript: How did it get decided, in the end?

Name: Rowan
Transcript: The rescue had a couple. They had a smallholding, no neighbours for about a mile, they'd had collies before, they'd had a nervous one. And the woman from the rescue rang and said, I think we might have someone, and I said yes before she'd told me anything else about them. Then I put the phone down and sat on the kitchen floor. And Skye came and put her head in my lap. Like she knew. She didn't know, she just saw me on the floor and came over. But it felt like she knew.

Name: Adam
Transcript: Can you tell me about the day she went?

Name: Rowan
Transcript: I drove her up there myself. They said I didn't have to, the rescue would do it, but I wanted to. Two hours in the car. She was always good in the car, she'd just sleep. And I talked to her the whole way, I don't even know what about. Rubbish, mostly. And when we got there they had this big field with sheep right at the far end, and she stood at the gate with her nose going, and she looked back at me once. Then she went off with the man to see the field. She didn't look back again. Which is what you'd want. I know that's what you'd want.

Name: Adam
Transcript: How long ago was that?

Name: Rowan
Transcript: End of June. So just over three months now.

Name: Adam
Transcript: And after she'd gone off to see the field?

Name: Rowan
Transcript: I sat in the car in their yard for a bit before I drove home. Twenty minutes, maybe. I wasn't crying. I thought I would and I didn't. I just felt very light, like my arms didn't have anything to hold. And then I drove home, and the flat was, it was just a flat. Her bowl was still on the floor because I hadn't thought to bring it. I've still got her bowl, actually. It's in the cupboard under the sink. I don't know why I've kept it.

Name: Adam
Transcript: What's it been like since?

Name: Rowan
Transcript: Quiet. Very quiet. I still wake up at quarter past five, three months on. Every day. I lie there and there's nothing to get up for, so I just lie there. They send me photos. She's on a sofa in one of them, which she was never allowed on with me, with her chin on a cushion looking really pleased with herself. And I look at that and think, good. Good, she's happy. And then I put the phone face down on the table for a bit.

Name: Adam
Transcript: What happens when you put the phone face down?

Name: Rowan
Transcript: I don't know, exactly. It's like I'm glad and something else at the same time, and the something else hasn't got a name yet. Everyone says she's better off. My sister says it, the rescue says it, I say it. I say it a lot, actually, out loud, to myself, in the kitchen. She's better off. And I think it's true. But I notice I have to keep saying it. If it was settled I wouldn't need to say it every day, would I.

Name: Adam
Transcript: Do you think about having another dog?

Name: Rowan
Transcript: People ask me that. My sister asks every time she rings. And I say not yet, which is true, but I don't know what yet means. Some days I think I'll never do it again, I couldn't go through it. Some days I'm on the rescue's page, looking. I haven't filled anything in. I think I'd want to know first whether I failed her or whether I did the right thing for her, and I don't know that, and I'm not sure anyone can tell me.

Name: Adam
Transcript: Is there anything about living with Skye that we haven't touched on?

Name: Rowan
Transcript: Only that she was a good dog. I want that said, because the way this has come out it sounds like she was a problem. She wasn't a problem. She was frightened. There's a difference. With me, in the flat, with the door shut, she was the gentlest thing. She'd bring me one sock in the morning. Never a pair, just the one, and drop it on the bed and wait. Every morning for eighteen months I got one sock. I still find odd socks in the washing and think of her. Stupid, really.

Name: Adam
Transcript: Thank you, Rowan. Is there anything else at all, before I stop the recording?

Name: Rowan
Transcript: No. No, I think that's everything.
